scenario_stem:
Ashcombe Pipe Organs Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by managing director Elena Vasquez, handcrafting bespoke pipe organs in a small workshop in Country X. Each organ is built to order, taking between 14 and 20 weeks to complete. The firm employs 24 skilled craftspeople and has 6 organs on its order book. Revenue last year was $1.8 million.

A luxury hotel group has offered a $420,000 contract to build a concert-hall pipe organ, which would take about 18 months and occupy 40% of workshop capacity. Alternatively, Elena could keep accepting chapel organ orders averaging $85,000 each and continue serving her existing customers. She must decide whether to accept the hotel contract, weighing the large upfront fee against her obligations to loyal clients.

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits of job production.
questions.model_answer: Each product is made to the customer's exact requirements, so quality tends to be high and buyers receive a unique, made-to-order item [1]. Skilled workers take pride in one-off craftsmanship, which can raise motivation and reduce labour turnover [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Product made to customer specification / unique product, high quality
Skilled, motivated workforce / workers take pride in one-off work

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why job production is suitable for building pipe organs.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Each pipe organ must be designed to fit the acoustics and dimensions of a particular building, so it cannot be mass-produced [k]. Job production builds every instrument to the customer's exact specification, which suits a $420,000 concert-hall commission [app]. Reason 2: Organ building relies on highly skilled craftspeople with specialist voicing and joinery skills [k]. This justifies keeping 24 skilled craftspeople in a small workshop rather than replacing labour with large-scale machinery [app].

knowledge_max_2: Every organ is unique / built to specification / cannot be mass-produced
Requires highly skilled craftspeople / specialist labour
application_max_2: Concert-hall organ is a one-off $420,000 commission needing exact specification
24 craftspeople, acoustics and size of the building

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of job production for Ashcombe Pipe Organs Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Output is slow, with every organ taking between 14 and 20 weeks to complete [k]. Tying up 40% of workshop capacity for about 18 months on the hotel project could delay the 6 organs on the order book [app], so regular chapel customers may lose patience and order from rivals instead [an]. Disadvantage 2: Unit costs are high because one organ is built at a time [k]. Craft wages and materials push chapel organs to an average of $85,000 each [app], so relatively few buyers can afford an organ, limiting the size of market the firm can serve [an].

knowledge_max_2: Job production is slow / low output rate
High unit costs / high wages for skilled craftspeople
application_max_2: 14-20 weeks per organ; 6 organs on the order book delayed
$85,000 average chapel organ price; 40% capacity used for 18 months
analysis_max_2: Delays to existing customers damages loyalty and could lose sales
High prices restrict demand / shrink the potential market

questions.question_text: Do you think Elena should accept the hotel contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for accepting: the hotel contract is worth $420,000, far above the $85,000 average chapel organ price, so revenue would rise sharply [k]. A concert-hall installation would showcase the firm's organs to a high-profile audience of wealthy clients [app]. This could generate prestigious future commissions and strengthen Ashcombe Pipe Organs Ltd as a premium organ builder [an]. Arguments against: the job occupies 40% of workshop capacity for about 18 months [k], during which the 6 organs on the order book and loyal chapel customers may face delays [app]. Losing those steady $85,000 orders could damage relationships built over 9 years and leave the firm over-dependent on one big client [an]. Overall, if the hotel agrees flexible scheduling that protects chapel orders, the cash value and prestige of the $420,000 contract make it worth accepting [eval]. However, if the hotel demands fixed exclusive use of the workshop, declining is the safer choice to retain loyal customers and steady revenue [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Job production can mean high revenue from one-off large orders / premium work
Job production ties up capacity and can cause bottlenecks / delays for existing customers
application_max_2: $420,000 contract vs $85,000 chapel organ average
40% capacity for 18 months; 6 organs on the order book; 9 years of relationships
analysis_max_2: Prestige and reputation gains could win future commissions
Delaying loyal customers risks lost sales and single-client dependence
evaluation_max_2: Conditional judgement based on flexibility of the hotel contract
Weighs a justified position citing stem figures; no single right answer required

scenario_stem:
Bramblewood Preserves is a partnership run by Diane Whitmore and Marcus Bell in Country X, producing bottled fruit jams and chutneys. The firm makes 8 flavours in batches of 2,400 jars, with each batch taking one full day on the shared kettle and filling line. It employs 14 workers and sold 310,000 jars last year at an average selling price of $3.20 per jar.

A national supermarket chain has offered a three-year contract for 60,000 jars of strawberry jam per month, but only if the firm guarantees monthly deliveries. Diane and Marcus debate whether to increase batch size and buy a second kettle for $55,000, or keep producing mainly through farmers' markets, where loyal stall customers pay full price. Either route would reshape the partnership.

questions.question_text: Identify two disadvantages of batch production.
questions.model_answer: Time is lost between batches when machinery must be reset, cleaned and switched to a different product [1]. Stock of finished goods or work-in-progress can build up between batches, raising storage costs and the risk of unsold output [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Setup / changeover time lost between batches
Work-in-progress or finished stock builds up / storage costs and risk of unsold stock

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of batch production for Bramblewood Preserves.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Batch production allows many different products to be made on shared equipment [k]. One kettle and filling line can produce all 8 flavours in runs of 2,400 jars, keeping fixed costs low for a small partnership [app]. Advantage 2: Batch production lets the firm switch easily when demand changes [k]. If strawberry sells faster than chutney, Diane and Marcus can allocate more batch days to strawberry and fewer to slow-selling flavours [app].

knowledge_max_2: Different products made on the same machinery / flexibility of product range
Easy to switch production when demand changes
application_max_2: 8 flavours produced on one shared kettle and filling line; batches of 2,400 jars
Strawberry vs chutney demand; farmers' markets vs supermarket

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of increasing batch size for the supermarket contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Larger batches spread setup costs across more jars [k]. Filling 60,000 jars a month in fewer, bigger runs would cut the cost per jar and help cover the $55,000 second kettle [app], which improves profit margins on the contract and frees cash for expansion [an]. Benefit 2: Bigger batches raise total capacity [k]. The existing line making 2,400 jars a day cannot reach 60,000 jars a month alone, so a second kettle lifts daily capacity and supports guaranteed monthly deliveries [app], reducing the risk of losing the three-year contract to a rival supplier [an].

knowledge_max_2: Larger batches spread fixed / setup costs over more units, lowering unit cost
Larger batches / extra capacity increase potential output
application_max_2: 60,000 jars per month for three years; $55,000 second kettle
Current line makes 2,400 jars per day, insufficient alone for 60,000 jars per month
analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs improve margins and cash for expansion
Extra capacity secures monthly deliveries and protects the contract from rivals

questions.question_text: Do you think Diane and Marcus should buy the second kettle and take the supermarket contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for taking the contract: it guarantees 60,000 jars per month for three years, far more than the 310,000 jars sold last year [k]. At $3.20 per jar, 60,000 jars gives monthly revenue of $192,000, dwarfing farmers' market sales [app]. This steady cash flow would repay the $55,000 kettle quickly and fund further growth [an]. Arguments against: relying on one supermarket hands the chain power to squeeze prices, and failing to deliver risks losing the contract and the kettle investment [k]. The firm may lose its farmers' market brand identity, with 8 flavours shrinking towards strawberry only [app]. Dependence on one buyer is dangerous if the chain cuts the contract after a year, leaving an expensive second kettle under-used [an]. Overall, with forecast revenue near $192,000 per month and a quick return on the investment, taking the contract is sensible provided they negotiate a price guarantee and keep some farmers' market presence [eval]. However, if the supermarket refuses price protection or demands exclusivity, remaining small protects margins and flexibility [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Large orders can guarantee revenue and support economies of larger batches
Dependence on one large buyer increases risk / customer has negotiating power
application_max_2: 60,000 jars per month x $3.20 = $192,000 per month; 310,000 jars last year
$55,000 second kettle; three-year contract; farmers' markets at risk
analysis_max_2: Steady cash flow aids investment and growth
Loss of brand identity and over-dependence on one buyer
evaluation_max_2: Conditional judgement; justified by citing revenue and capital-cost figures
Notes circumstances under which decision should be reversed

scenario_stem:
SoftWeave Paper Products Ltd, a private limited company in Country X, manufactures paper tissues and kitchen roll on one continuous flow production line. The line runs 16 hours a day, 6 days a week, producing 1,200 packs per hour, and employs 38 machine operators plus 6 maintenance staff. Last year the firm sold 9.6 million packs at $2.40 each.

Demand is rising and SoftWeave is considering adding a second continuous line costing $1.15 million, rather than paying overtime or outsourcing overflow to a competitor's factory. The new line would double capacity to 2,400 packs per hour but would deepen dependence on a single supplier of recycled paper pulp. The directors must decide by next month, before the autumn peak trading season begins, and want a recommendation backed by the figures.

questions.question_text: State two advantages of flow production.
questions.model_answer: Flow production can produce very large quantities quickly through a continuous process [1]. Unit costs are low because output is high and machinery keeps running, spreading fixed costs [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Very high output / continuous production
Low unit cost / fixed costs spread over huge output

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why flow production suits SoftWeave Paper Products Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Paper tissues are a standardised, identical product sold in huge volumes, which suits continuous production [k]. The line already outputs 1,200 packs per hour and SoftWeave sold 9.6 million packs last year, volumes that job or batch production could not match economically [app]. Reason 2: Flow production uses capital equipment intensively with very few changeovers [k]. With only tissues and kitchen roll to make, the single line and its 38 machine operators can run 16 hours a day without costly resetting [app].

knowledge_max_2: Standardised, identical products suit flow production
Capital intensive, few changeovers / machinery used continuously
application_max_2: 1,200 packs per hour; 9.6 million packs sold; $2.40 per pack
38 machine operators; 16 hours a day line running tissues and kitchen roll

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of adding a second flow production line.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: The $1.15 million investment raises fixed costs sharply [k]. If demand dipped below the doubled capacity of 2,400 packs per hour, the new line would still incur machine and building costs [app], squeezing profit margins and lengthening the time needed to recoup the money invested [an]. Risk 2: A second line deepens dependence on a single supplier of recycled paper pulp [k]. Any disruption to pulp deliveries would halt twice as much output as before, stopping both lines together [app], which could lose key supermarket customers to rivals during the outage [an].

knowledge_max_2: High capital cost / fixed costs rise with a second line
Dependence on one supplier / supply disruption risk
application_max_2: $1.15 million cost; doubled capacity of 2,400 packs per hour
Single supplier of recycled paper pulp; both lines depend on pulp
analysis_max_2: Idle capacity squeezes margins / delays recouping the investment
Losing pulp supply halts all output, risking customers

questions.question_text: Do you think SoftWeave should add the second production line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for adding the line: demand is rising and the present line already runs 16 hours a day, 6 days a week, so it has no spare capacity [k]. A second line doubling capacity to 2,400 packs per hour could lift sales beyond 9.6 million packs without overtime or outsourcing premiums [app]. Higher output would lower average costs and could win new supermarket contracts [an]. Arguments against: outsourcing overflow is flexible, so SoftWeave pays only for the output it needs and avoids the $1.15 million outlay and the single-supplier pulp risk [k]. If demand fell, outsourcing could simply be cut back [app]. Keeping cash free also funds marketing and shields the firm from over-commitment to one pulp supplier [an]. Overall, if rising demand is confirmed by firm supermarket orders, the second line offers the lowest long-run unit cost and is worth funding [eval]. However, if demand is seasonal or unproven, outsourcing overflow first limits risk until the trend is certain [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Flow production lowers unit cost at high volumes / justifies investment
Outsourcing offers flexibility without capital outlay
application_max_2: 16 hours a day, 6 days a week, 1,200 packs per hour, 9.6 million packs
$1.15 million cost; 2,400 packs per hour capacity; single pulp supplier
analysis_max_2: Lower average costs and new contracts from expanded capacity
Flexibility of outsourcing vs fixed commitment and supplier risk
evaluation_max_2: Justified conditional judgement based on evidence of demand
Reversal condition stated if demand is unproven

scenario_stem:
Calver Caravans Ltd manufactures recreational caravans in a large factory in Country X. Currently, 42 workers operate as one long flow line, fitting panels, wiring and interiors in sequence. Workers wait on the previous stage 11% of the time, quality complaints cost $18,000 last year, and the line produced 380 caravans in total at an average cost of $9,800 per unit, below the target margin.

The production manager proposes replacing the flow line with 6 self-contained cells, each staffed by 7 multi-skilled workers building one caravan from shell to finish. The changeover would cost $140,000 and take 6 weeks, but each cell could complete a caravan in 26 working days and fix defects inside the cell. Initial staff training would take 5 days per worker.

questions.question_text: Define 'cell production'.
questions.model_answer: Cell production is a method of production where the process is split into groups (cells) of workers, each responsible for completing a whole product or a major part of it [1]. Each cell is self-managing and responsible for quality at its own stage [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Production split into groups/cells of workers completing whole products or major parts
Cells are self-managing / responsible for quality at their stage

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of cell production for Calver Caravans Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Cell production reduces waiting and movement between stages [k]. With 42 workers split into 6 self-contained cells, each caravan is built start-to-finish in one place, cutting the 11% idle time found on the flow line [app]. Advantage 2: Communication within a small cell is easier [k]. A 7-person cell can spot and fix wiring and panel faults immediately instead of passing defects down the line [app].

knowledge_max_2: Less waiting/movement between stages / reduced idle time
Easier communication within small teams / defects fixed at source
application_max_2: 42 workers into 6 cells; eliminates 11% waiting time
7 multi-skilled workers per cell; wiring and panel faults spotted early

questions.question_text: Explain two ways cell production could improve quality and costs at Calver Caravans Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Quality improvement: each cell owns the caravan from shell to finish and checks its own work [k]. Caravans completed in 26 working days within one cell are inspected by the same team that built them, so wiring and panel faults are caught earlier [app], reducing rework and warranty claims after delivery [an]. Cost improvement: multi-skilled workers can cover several tasks [k]. Coverage within each 7-person cell keeps output near 380 caravans a year flowing without overtime or temporary labour [app], lowering the average cost below $9,800 per caravan [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cells responsible for quality at their stage / own-check inspection
Multi-skilled teams cover absences / flexibility of labour
application_max_2: 26 working days per caravan; faults caught within the cell
7-person cells keep output near 380 caravans flowing
analysis_max_2: Earlier fault detection cuts rework and warranty costs
Less overtime/temp labour lowers average cost per caravan

questions.question_text: Do you think Calver Caravans Ltd should replace the flow line with cell production? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for switching: cell production attacks the 11% idle time caused by waiting between flow-line stages [k]. Each of the 6 cells can build a whole caravan in 26 working days with defect-fixing inside the cell, cutting rework and potentially lifting output above 380 caravans a year [app]. Lower unit costs would strengthen competitiveness against imports [an]. Arguments against: the switch costs $140,000 and takes 6 weeks [k], during which production could fall and the order book suffer delays [app]. Multi-skilling 42 workers requires training time and some staff may resist the change [an]. Overall, because cells remove the 11% idle time and embed quality at a one-off cost of $140,000, the change is justified if cash flow allows and workers support it [eval]. However, if demand is uncertain or workers resist strongly, introducing cells one at a time over six months is the lower-risk route [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cell production reduces idle time/waiting and improves quality ownership
Switching production methods involves capital cost, disruption and training
application_max_2: 11% idle time; 26 working days per caravan; 6 cells of 7 workers
$140,000 cost; 6 weeks changeover; current output 380 caravans at $9,800
analysis_max_2: Lower unit cost strengthens competitiveness vs imports
Disruption, training cost and staff resistance could delay the gains
evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement based on cash flow and worker buy-in
Alternative phased implementation acknowledges uncertainty

scenario_stem:
Suncourt Flowers is a family-owned company in Country X growing cut roses and lilies for 3 national supermarket chains. It currently harvests each morning and stores up to 4 days of unsold flowers in a chilled cold store costing $3,600 per week to run. Last year wastage from unsold stock was 9% of output, and at peak the cold store holds $28,000 of flowers grown on 6 hectares.

The operations manager proposes switching to just-in-time, harvesting and delivering twice daily so supermarkets receive flowers within 8 hours of cutting. Hauliers would charge $700 per extra trip. The chains reserve the right to cancel standing orders at 48 hours notice. Suncourt's two regular hauliers need reliability checks before any change is agreed.

questions.question_text: State two advantages of low inventory levels for a business.
questions.model_answer: Storage and warehousing costs fall because the business holds little stock [1]. Less working capital is tied up in unsold goods, and waste from obsolete or unsold stock is reduced [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Lower storage / warehousing costs
Less capital tied up in stock / less obsolete or wasted stock

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of switching to just-in-time for Suncourt Flowers.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Just-in-time would cut cold-store costs [k]. Harvesting and delivering twice daily so flowers reach shelves within 8 hours could remove the $3,600 weekly cold-store cost and shrink the $28,000 of flowers held at peak [app]. Benefit 2: Just-in-time also reduces waste [k]. The 9% of output lost to unsold stock should fall because flowers are cut only to known demand [app].

knowledge_max_2: JIT reduces storage / warehousing costs
JIT reduces waste / obsolete and unsold stock
application_max_2: Cold store costs $3,600 per week; holds $28,000 of flowers at peak
9% of output wasted; twice daily harvest to demand

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of just-in-time for Suncourt Flowers.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: Production for delivery can be stopped by transport failures [k]. Harvesting and delivering twice daily means any missed trip or vehicle breakdown leaves the supermarkets without flowers and Suncourt with no route to market for that day's cut [app], risking lost sales and penalties from the 3 national supermarket chains [an]. Risk 2: JIT depends on reliable partners and offers no protection against cancellations [k]. If a chain cancels its standing order at 48 hours notice, cut flowers already harvested for that order may have no other buyer [app], turning low stock levels into immediate write-offs with no time to find new customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Supply or transport delays can halt production / delivery
Dependence on reliable suppliers/customers; no fallback for cancellations
application_max_2: Twice daily harvests; $700 per extra haulier trip; 3 supermarket chains
Chains can cancel at 48 hours notice; flowers perish quickly
analysis_max_2: Missed deliveries mean lost sales and damaged supermarket relationships
Late cancellations create unsaleable perishable stock with no fallback

questions.question_text: Do you think Suncourt Flowers should switch to just-in-time? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for switching: JIT removes the $3,600 weekly cold-store cost and shrinks the $28,000 peak stock, freeing working capital [k]. Fresher flowers within 8 hours of cutting improve shelf life and would delight supermarket buyers, strengthening the 3 contracts [app]. Higher quality and lower waste could lift margins on every stem sold [an]. Arguments against: JIT leaves the firm exposed to haulier delays and to chains cancelling at 48 hours notice [k]. Extra haulier trips at $700 add cost, and one missed twice-daily delivery could sour relationships with supermarkets [app]. Cancellation shortly after cutting could leave perishable stock unsold despite low inventory [an]. Overall, JIT suits a high-frequency, perishable product with 9% wastage and costly storage, so adopting it is justified provided hauliers prove reliable and chains sign minimum-order commitments [eval]. However, if the chains refuse minimum-order terms, holding a small back-up supply of one day's flowers is prudent insurance [eval].

knowledge_max_2: JIT lowers storage costs and waste, suits perishable high-turnover goods
JIT risks halted operations and dependence on reliable supply and demand
application_max_2: $3,600 per week cold store; $28,000 peak stock; 9% wastage; 8 hours freshness
$700 per extra trip; 48 hours notice cancellations; 3 national chains
analysis_max_2: Lower costs and fresher stock strengthen margins and contracts
Transport failures and cancellations risk lost sales and unsold stock
evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement; conditions attached to the decision
Insurance via minimal back-up supply acknowledges residual risk

scenario_stem:
Rushton Paper Mill Ltd, a private limited company in Country X, produces 26,000 tonnes of kraft paper a year on a 10-year-old machine. Last year the mill scrapped 2,080 tonnes as trimmings and off-spec rolls, equal to 8% of output, and spent $150,000 disposing of waste. Worker morale is low, the mill employs 120 workers on 3 shifts, and shop-floor ideas are rarely collected.

The operations director proposes a kaizen programme of small, continuous improvements, with weekly team meetings and a suggestion scheme, targeting a 25% cut in waste over 12 months. The alternative is a single immediate investment of $250,000 in a new laser trimmer, which would cut trimming waste by 40% at once but require board approval and about 8 weeks of commissioning time.

questions.question_text: Identify two ways kaizen can reduce waste in a factory.
questions.model_answer: Workers suggest small, continuous improvements to processes and layouts, reducing unnecessary motion, waiting and handling [1]. Regular review and team feedback spot defects early, lowering reject rates and scrap [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Small continuous worker-led improvements to processes / layouts
Early spotting of defects / reduced motion, waiting, handling and rejects

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why kaizen could suit Rushton Paper Mill Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Kaizen costs little to start [k]. It avoids the $250,000 upfront laser trimmer and asks only for meeting time and a suggestion scheme, which suits a mill watching cash flow [app]. Reason 2: Kaizen empowers workers and lifts morale [k]. With morale low and ideas rarely collected, weekly team meetings give operators a voice, raising engagement and quality awareness across the shop floor [app].

knowledge_max_2: Kaizen involves low-cost, continuous small improvements
Kaizen involves and motivates all employees / raises morale
application_max_2: Avoids $250,000 laser trimmer; low-cost meetings and suggestion scheme
Low morale and rarely collected shop-floor ideas

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of achieving a 25% cut in waste through kaizen.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Waste disposal and lost material costs fall [k]. Cutting 8% wastage by a quarter saves about 520 tonnes of paper a year and reduces part of the $150,000 disposal bill [app], directly lifting profit without new machinery or debt [an]. Benefit 2: A 25% waste cut frees up machine capacity [k]. With 26,000 tonnes sold a year, reclaiming 520 tonnes of sellable paper raises effective output and reduces reliance on the 10-year-old machine running flat out [app], helping the mill meet orders on time and avoid lost custom [an].

knowledge_max_2: Less waste lowers disposal / material / scrap costs
Less waste raises effective capacity / output from same resources
application_max_2: 25% of 2,080 tonnes = 520 tonnes saved; part of $150,000 disposal bill
26,000 tonnes annual output; 10-year-old machine
analysis_max_2: Lower costs directly improve profit without debt
Extra capacity helps meet orders and protects customer relationships

questions.question_text: Do you think Rushton Paper Mill Ltd should adopt kaizen instead of buying the laser trimmer? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for kaizen: it attacks the same 8% wastage at low cost, avoiding the $250,000 trimmer outlay [k]. Weekly team meetings and a suggestion scheme build a culture of continuous improvement and lift morale on the shop floor [app]. Because kaizen is gradual, savings build over 12 months without debt or long machine downtime [an]. Arguments for the trimmer: it would cut trimming waste by 40% at once, beating the 25% kaizen target in year one [k]. A full year of gradual kaizen may under-deliver if meetings fade or workers mistrust the scheme [app]. Kaizen also demands sustained management commitment, whereas the trimmer is a one-off purchase [an]. Overall, kaizen is the better first step given its low cost, morale gains and 25% target, with the trimmer deferred until 12-month results are visible [eval]. However, if the board demands a guaranteed, fast 40% waste cut and cash is available, buying the trimmer now is the stronger choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Kaizen gives steady low-cost improvement with worker involvement
Capital investment gives immediate, guaranteed but costly waste reduction
application_max_2: 8% waste; 25% kaizen target; $150,000 disposal bill
$250,000 laser trimmer cutting waste 40% at once
analysis_max_2: Kaizen builds culture and avoids debt; savings are gradual and uncertain
Trimmer gives certainty and speed but high cost and less culture change
evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement; both options weighed with stem figures
States the circumstance under which the alternative is preferred

scenario_stem:
Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making hand trowels, forks and rakes. Workers move parts between 3 separate buildings, and changeovers between product sizes take 55 minutes. Scrap from metal offcuts cost $95,000 last year, and late deliveries cost $30,000 in penalty fees. Orders are forecast at 38,000 units next year, with 4 national retailers already on the order book.

The owner is considering adopting lean production: cutting waste, reorganising the workflow into a single flow and involving workers in continuous improvement, at an initial cost of $60,000 for training and layout changes. The alternative is to carry on as before and rely on a new sales manager to boost revenue within 6 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'lean production'.
questions.model_answer: Lean production is an approach to production that aims to reduce or eliminate waste of all kinds, such as time, materials, stock, movement and defects, from the production process [1]. It also aims to produce only what is needed, when it is needed, using fewer resources [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Approach aimed at eliminating/reducing waste (time, materials, stock, movement, defects)
Produces only what is needed, when needed, using fewer resources

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of lean production for Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Lean production reduces waste and cost [k]. Cutting the $95,000 metal-offcut scrap through tighter layouts and worker suggestions would directly improve profit [app]. Benefit 2: Lean production shortens changeover times [k]. Reducing the 55 minutes needed to change between trowel, fork and rake sizes lets Thornfield switch products faster and serve varied orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lean reduces waste and costs
Lean reduces changeover / setup times and speeds flow
application_max_2: $95,000 scrap from metal offcuts
55-minute changeovers between trowel, fork and rake sizes

questions.question_text: Explain two ways lean production could help Thornfield meet next year's forecast of 38,000 units.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Lean removes delays between processes [k]. Reorganising into a single flow instead of 3 separate buildings cuts transport time and waiting between stages [app], so throughput rises without overtime and the 38,000 units forecast becomes achievable [an]. Way 2: Lean reduces late deliveries [k]. Smoother flow and faster 55-minute changeovers mean orders ship on time, helping avoid repeat $30,000 penalty fees [app], which keeps key retail customers loyal and protects future orders [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lean reduces waiting/transport/movement waste between processes
Lean smooths flow, reduces delays and late deliveries
application_max_2: Single flow replaces 3 separate buildings; throughput rises
55-minute changeovers; avoids $30,000 penalty fees
analysis_max_2: Higher throughput without overtime supports 38,000 units forecast
On-time delivery protects customer loyalty and repeat orders

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd should adopt lean production? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for adopting lean: it tackles waste directly, with $95,000 scrap, 55-minute changeovers and $30,000 penalty fees all reducible [k]. A one-off $60,000 for training and layout changes could recover its cost within a year and lift capacity towards 38,000 units [app]. Involving workers in continuous improvement should raise motivation and ownership on the shop floor [an]. Arguments for the sales-manager alternative: that route could boost revenue quickly without reorganising production or spending $60,000 upfront [k]. If workers resist change or meetings fade, lean savings may not materialise [app]. A new sales manager may also open new retail accounts that increase orders immediately [an]. Overall, lean production attacks the root causes of waste and should underpin sustainable growth towards 38,000 units, so adopting it now is justified if the owner commits to training and follow-through [eval]. However, if cash is tight, rolling the changes out gradually, department by department, limits risk while still capturing savings [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Lean addresses root-cause waste and can be employee-driven
Lean carries upfront cost, culture change and uncertain payoff
application_max_2: $95,000 scrap; $30,000 penalty fees; 55-minute changeovers
$60,000 training and layout cost; 38,000 units forecast
analysis_max_2: Sustainable cost and capacity gains underpin growth
Quick revenue boost possible but does not fix waste; risk of failed rollout
evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement citing investment cost and waste figures
Acknowledges risk and proposes staged alternative

scenario_stem:
Spinwell Vinyl Ltd is a private limited company in Country X pressing vinyl records. It currently presses in batches of 2,000 records, changing labels and jackets between runs; the machine presses 4,000 records per working day and the firm sold 820,000 records last year. Independent artists order runs of 500-1,000 records, paying premium prices. Its cutting machines are serviced every 6 weeks under a fixed maintenance contract.

A major label has offered a three-year contract for 120,000 records per month of a new compilation album, the largest single order in the firm's history. Spinwell could keep batch production, adding night shifts at overtime cost, or invest $900,000 in a dedicated flow line pressing only that title at 15,000 records per day. The board meets next week to decide.

questions.question_text: Identify two disadvantages of flow production.
questions.model_answer: Flow production is inflexible, making it expensive and time-consuming to switch the product made [1]. It requires very large capital investment and high output volumes to justify the specialist machinery [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Inflexible / hard and costly to switch products
High capital investment / needs high volumes to break even

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why batch production suits independent record orders.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Batch production can switch between small, varied runs [k]. Runs of 500-1,000 records for independent artists need different labels and jackets, and changing over between batches makes these variations practical [app]. Reason 2: Batch production suits premium-priced, lower-volume work [k]. Pressing 500-1,000 at a time avoids overproducing unsold records while capturing the premium prices independent artists will pay [app].

knowledge_max_2: Batch production handles small varied runs / changeovers between products
Batch suits premium-price, low-volume work / avoids overproduction
application_max_2: 500-1,000 record runs need different labels and jackets
Premium prices paid by independent artists

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of investing in the dedicated flow line.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A flow line slashes unit cost for the compilation [k]. Pressing 15,000 records per day of a single title removes the repeated changeovers of labels and jackets that slow batch runs today [app], so the very large 120,000 records per month contract becomes highly profitable [an]. Benefit 2: A flow line guarantees the label's monthly volumes [k]. At 15,000 records per day the line completes 120,000 records in 8 working days [app], giving the major label dependable supply throughout its three-year contract [an].

knowledge_max_2: Flow production lowers unit cost at high volume / no changeovers
Flow production guarantees supply / dependable high output
application_max_2: 15,000 records per day of one title; no label/jacket changeovers
120,000 records in 8 working days; 120,000 per month demand
analysis_max_2: Lower unit cost makes the compilation contract highly profitable
Dependable supply secures the three-year contract and future business

questions.question_text: Do you think Spinwell Vinyl Ltd should invest $900,000 in the dedicated flow line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for the flow line: the three-year contract for 120,000 records per month guarantees predictable, enormous volume that batch production with changeovers cannot match [k]. The flow line at 15,000 records per day finishes the monthly quota in 8 working days, leaving capacity to serve other clients [app]. Lower unit costs would transform margins on the compilation and attract future major-label work [an]. Arguments against: the $900,000 outlay ties up cash in one title for one customer, and a flow line is inflexible [k]. Batch production with night shifts keeps flexibility to serve independent artists ordering 500-1,000 records at premium prices [app]. A compilation flop would leave a costly dedicated line under-used, dragging down profit [an]. Overall, because the contract alone amounts to 1.44 million records a year against only 820,000 sold last year, a dedicated flow line is justified provided the label signs a firm minimum-purchase clause [eval]. However, if the label will not commit beyond one year, staying with flexible batch production plus night shifts is the safer option [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Dedicated flow line suits very high-volume, stable demand
Batch keeps flexibility for varied, premium-priced small runs
application_max_2: 120,000 per month x 36 months; 15,000/day = 8 days to fulfil; $900,000
820,000 records last year; 500-1,000 artist runs at premium prices
analysis_max_2: Lower unit cost and guaranteed supply win profit and future contracts
Single-customer, single-title dependence risks stranded investment if demand falls
evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement; compares 1.44 million contract volume vs 820,000 past sales
Stated reversal condition if contract commitment is weak

scenario_stem:
CaseCraft Ltd is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing phone cases under contract for 2 smartphone brands. Eight months ago it adopted just-in-time, holding almost no stock, and it now orders moulded parts from a single overseas supplier with a 12-week lead time and no local alternative.

Two supplier failures have since halted the assembly line for 3 days each, costing about $96,000 in lost output and forcing air-freighted parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment. The brands pay on a net-30 basis, which squeezes cash flow further. The operations manager, who joined 6 months ago, now debates abandoning just-in-time and rebuilding a 3-week stock of moulded parts costing $120,000, or keeping just-in-time and qualifying a second overseas supplier before the next smartphone model launch.

questions.question_text: Outline two disadvantages of just-in-time production.
questions.model_answer: If suppliers fail to deliver on time, production must stop because there is no stock to fall back on [1]. The business becomes heavily dependent on reliable suppliers, and any disruption can halt output completely [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Supply delays halt / stop production with no stock fallback
Heavy dependence on reliable suppliers

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of just-in-time shown by CaseCraft's experience.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: Just-in-time leaves no stock to absorb supplier disruption [k]. Both halts followed supplier failures, and with a 12-week lead time CaseCraft could not quickly replace moulded parts from scratch [app]. Risk 2: A single overseas supplier creates dangerous dependence [k]. The need to air-freight parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment shows how one failing source can sharply raise costs and stress the two smartphone brands [app].

knowledge_max_2: Supply disruption halts production when no stock is held
Dependence on a single/unreliable supplier is risky
application_max_2: 12-week lead time; line halted for 3 days each time
Air-freighted parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of qualifying a second overseas supplier while keeping just-in-time.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A second supplier reduces the chance of a halted line [k]. If one supplier fails, CaseCraft can switch orders across, avoiding 3-day stoppages like the two that cost $96,000 in lost output [app], protecting the two smartphone contracts and future renewals [an]. Benefit 2: A second supplier keeps the benefits of just-in-time [k]. Just-in-time still avoids the $120,000 needed to rebuild a 3-week stock, plus storage costs [app], so the firm keeps its lean cash flow while gaining resilience [an].

knowledge_max_2: Multiple suppliers reduce risk of stoppage / increase resilience
Qualifying a second supplier preserves low-stock / lean advantages
application_max_2: Two halts cost $96,000; avoiding repeat losses protects contracts
Avoids $120,000 3-week stock and storage costs
analysis_max_2: Protects the two smartphone contracts and reputation
Maintains low working capital and lean cash flow

questions.question_text: Do you think CaseCraft Ltd should abandon just-in-time? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for abandoning: two supplier failures in 8 months stopped the line for 6 days in total and cost $96,000 in lost output plus $18,000 air-freight bills [k]. Rebuilding a 3-week stock of parts costing $120,000 would let the line run through most disruptions and protect the two smartphone contracts [app]. Predictability and customer trust may outweigh stock-holding costs [an]. Arguments against abandoning: a 3-week stock ties up $120,000 that could be used elsewhere and adds storage costs, eroding the savings just-in-time created [k]. Qualifying a second overseas supplier attacks the same risk at lower cost while keeping working capital free [app]. Large stock also raises obsolescence risk for phone-specific parts [an]. Overall, abandoning just-in-time entirely is not justified; qualifying a second supplier plus a small emergency stock of critical parts is cheaper and safer than either extreme [eval]. However, if no second supplier can be qualified within 3 months, rebuilding the 3-week stock is a necessary stopgap [eval].

knowledge_max_2: JIT risk: halted production, dependence on suppliers
Stock holding costs: capital tied up, storage, obsolescence
application_max_2: Two halts x 3 days; $96,000 lost output; $18,000 air-freight
$120,000 3-week stock; 12-week lead time; 8 months experience
analysis_max_2: Stock gives predictability and protects customer contracts
Second supplier preserves lean benefits at lower cost; obsolescence risk of stock
evaluation_max_2: Justified conditional judgement favouring second supplier / small emergency stock
Stated fallback if supplier cannot be qualified quickly

scenario_stem:
Calloway Rods is a sole-trader fishing-rod workshop in Country X run by Sam Whitaker, building bespoke trout and salmon rods. Each rod is made to the angler's specification in about 7 days, sells at $340, and the workshop produced 260 rods last year with a 6-week waiting list and a part-time assistant who varnishes each rod.

Sam's supplier of hand-built cork grips has cut prices for identical grip designs ordered in batches. Local angling shops have asked to stock 3 standard models. Sam could keep full job production, switch the 3 standard models to batches of 40 and keep bespoke work on top, or go fully batch and drop custom orders completely, ending a decade of one-off builds. The shops want an answer within 3 months.

questions.question_text: Outline two advantages of batch production.
questions.model_answer: Batch production allows a range of different products to be made on shared machines, keeping some flexibility between runs [1]. Unit costs are lower than job production because larger quantities spread fixed and setup costs [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Different products made in batches on shared machinery / flexibility of range
Lower unit cost than job production / setup costs spread over batch

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why batch production might help Calloway Rods.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Batch production lowers unit costs for standard lines [k]. Making 3 standard models in batches of 40 would spread labour and machine time across 120 rods, cutting average cost per rod compared with one-off builds [app]. Reason 2: Batch production can supply local angling shops reliably [k]. Stocking 3 standard models in predictable batches of 40 matches exactly what the shops have asked for and relieves the 6-week waiting list [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower unit cost from larger runs / shared fixed costs
Predictable stock supply for retailers
application_max_2: 3 standard models x 40 = 120 rods per batch cycle
Angling shops asked for 3 standard models; 6-week waiting list

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Calloway Rods could face if it switched fully to batch production.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Unique bespoke work would disappear [k]. Dropping custom orders means giving up the $340 bespoke trout and salmon rods and the loyal customers behind the 6-week waiting list [app], shrinking the firm's premium reputation with serious anglers [an]. Problem 2: Batch production risks unsold stock [k]. If the 3 standard models do not sell in batches of 40, capital is tied up in rods that angling shops cannot shift [app], raising storage costs and waste if designs fall out of fashion [an].

knowledge_max_2: Loss of custom/bespoke work and premium reputation
Risk of unsold stock / capital tied up in batches
application_max_2: $340 bespoke trout and salmon rods; 6-week waiting list
3 standard models in batches of 40 held as stock
analysis_max_2: Eroding bespoke reputation reduces premium pricing power
Unsold batches tie up cash and raise storage/obsolescence costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Sam should switch the three standard models to batch production alongside the bespoke work? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for switching: producing 3 standard models in batches of 40 spreads setup costs, frees capacity for bespoke rods and shortens the 6-week waiting list [k]. Supplier discounts on identical hand-built cork grips ordered in batches cut material costs further [app]. The angling shops' request widens the market beyond the 260 rods sold last year [an]. Arguments against: splitting production could dilute the bespoke reputation that supports $340 pricing [k]. Batch runs of 40 unsold models tie up cash, and savings only materialise if grips are ordered for proven demand [app]. Overproducing one design would leave expensive unsold stock [an]. Overall, adding 3 standard batch models alongside bespoke work captures shop demand and supplier discounts without abandoning the firm's identity, so the partial switch is justified [eval]. However, Sam should keep batches small and monitor sell-through before expanding, protecting workshop flexibility [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Batch suits standard models / spreads setup costs, frees capacity
Risks: diluted bespoke identity, unsold stock, tied-up capital
application_max_2: Batches of 40 for 3 standard models; 6-week waiting list; 260 rods last year
Supplier discounts on identical cork grips; $340 bespoke price
analysis_max_2: Wider market and lower costs while retaining bespoke identity
Overproduction and reputation dilution risk if demand misjudged
evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement favouring partial switch
Safeguard suggested: small batches and sell-through monitoring
